blocks.text:
## Trip highlights

In Bogotá, you’ll visit La Candelaria, the Gold Museum, the Casa de la Moneda, the Botero collection and Plaza de Bolívar. A separate day takes you outside the capital to Zipaquirá and the Guatavita Lagoon, which is associated with the legend of El Dorado.

The next part of the trip takes you to La Macarena, where the programme depends on permits from the environmental authorities. On the day you arrive, you’ll visit one of several alternative natural sites. The following days are set aside for routes in the Caño Cristales area itself.

Caño Cristales is known for the bright colours that appear in the water during certain months of the year. The aquatic plant Macarenia clavigera gives the riverbed shades of red, pink, yellow, green and blue. The routes take you past natural pools and cascades, through jungle and across rocky terrain.

After returning to Bogotá, you’ll continue to Pereira. You’ll visit the Cocora Valley and Salento and follow a nature trail to see the wax palms. The next day, you’ll visit a coffee farm and head to the Santa Rosa de Cabal hot springs.

The final days are on the Caribbean coast. In Cartagena, a sightseeing tour takes in San Felipe de Barajas Fortress and the historic centre. You’ll then spend a full day in the Rosario Islands.

## How the nature portion of the trip works

The route at Caño Cristales can vary from one visit to the next. Environmental authorities and the managers of the protected areas assign the trails. The programme sets out the days, transport, meals and overall sequence in advance, while the current permit determines which part of La Macarena you can visit.

This also applies on the day you arrive. You’ll head to one of three alternative sites away from the main channel of Caño Cristales: Caño Cristalitos, Caño Piedra or the Río Bajo Lozada. Over the following days, you’ll visit the authorised sections of Caño Cristales. This helps spread visitors across the area and meet conservation requirements.

After flying to La Macarena, you’ll travel by boat on the Guayabero River and by 4x4. On foot, the routes cross jungle and rocky ground and pass natural pools and cascades. Lunches on these outings are included, and one is served wrapped in bijao leaves to reduce single-use packaging.
